en: The First Chapter: An Auspicious Invocation and the Origin of Āyurveda.
The venerable Tīrthādhipa, the conqueror of enemies and the Bull (Vṛṣabha), appeared, his footstool honored by the mass of rays from the rubies in the crests of the lords of gods, asuras, and men.
The direct, non-causal, and sole kinsman of the three worlds. The essential meaning: [The Hindi commentary was not digitized.
A prayer to Lord Ādinātha.

Having approached that Lord of Tīrthas, whose form was encompassed by the power of true miracles and other wonders, they bowed their heads and offered salutations with devotion through the three modes of action.
Bharateśvara and the others asked about all of this in such a manner.
[Verse 2] The essential meaning (bhāvārtha): People who have conceived an excessive attachment toward the lands of enjoyment in previous lives... [The Hindi commentary was not digitized.]
Having experienced divine bliss with all great enjoyments offered by the wish-fulfilling trees, those of great merit returned once more to human state and attained the desired happiness of heaven.
The meaning of the verse:
Here, the classes of embodied beings who are born with their feet upward (inverted) possess superior merit and possess great lifespans that cannot be diminished.

Others in this world, whose supreme lifespans were subject to reduction, experienced great fear here due to the provocation of their own faults. 4. The essential meaning (bhāvārtha): [The Hindi commentary was not digitized.]

O Lord! You alone are the refuge for those who have come to you for shelter— those of us here in this land of action whose minds are agitated and who are oppressed by cold, heat, and the downpour of snow.
Of those who, over the course of time, were intent on eating coarse food; [this is] the essential meaning— of those who were exceedingly distressed by the fear of various kinds of diseases.
O Lord of the World! For us who do not understand the etymology of great medicines, what action can there be for those afflicted here, as we explain the method for protecting their health? 6.
The essential meaning:
Having informed the Lord of His divine voice, [he did so] for the sake of the welfare of the entire world.
While the eminent leaders, headed by the Gaṇadharas, remained silent in that great assembly, a melodious voice accompanied by divine resonance issued forth from the goddess Varadevī.
The essential meaning— [the Hindi commentary was not digitized].
Regarding the description of the four categories of reality, first of all, the definition of the Puruṣa is stated:
She then spoke this, which indicates omniscience: the medicinal herbs, the distinctions of all times, and in brief, the fourfold totality of all things.
The essential meaning:
The traditional transmission of the science of Āyurveda,
which consists of the collection of ultimate truths revealed by the divine voice.
Thus, the Gaṇadhara learned everything directly;
afterwards, the sages of pure intellect, whose minds were cleansed by half of the eight [qualities], learned the expansion of words as prescribed by the Lord of the Gaṇas.
The essential meaning:
Thus, [the path] established by the interval between the Jinas is attained—
extensive, undisturbed, and profound in its significance.

That entire eternal [teaching] of Svayambhū was heard directly by those whose ears were the scriptures from the Śruta-kevalins. The meaning of the intent (bhāvārtha): [The Hindi commentary was not digitized.]
The author's promise:
[I shall describe] either a tiny spray issuing from a rising wave within the ocean of the nectar of the Victor’s emerging teachings, or...

We shall speak of that which is the sole abode of the welfare of all the world, renowned as the "Bringer of Auspiciousness," and endowed with its intended meaning. (11) The essential meaning (*bhāvārtha*)— [the Hindi commentary was not digitized].
The purpose of composing this work is neither due to excessive eloquence, nor from pride in poetic skill,
nor for the sake of shattering the arrogance of other treatises.
However, considering it to be his own penance, he will follow the excellent path of the Teacher and accomplish that task. The essential meaning (bhāvārtha): [The Hindi commentary was not digitized.]
Others say that self-study is the root of all austerities,
and I consider it to be primarily characterized by affection for the best of physicians; therefore, I shall strive with effort in the practice of austerity itself.
Now begins [this work], which correctly brings about the happiness of both oneself and others.
The essential meaning (bhāvārtha): Durjananindā (Censure of the Wicked).
Here too, there are many who are crooked by nature,
of evil vision, double-tongued, impelled by wicked thoughts, intent upon seeking out faults, and harmful to others.
Those lowest of men are comparable to fierce serpents. (14) The essential meaning— [The Hindi commentary was not digitized.
Furthermore, some possess qualities that are esteemed within their own homes, yet [regarding] others...
Indeed, there is no fault in that which is censured by those who know all things;
rather, it is the very nature of the evil-minded—characterized by malice toward others, backbiting, and harsh speech. || 15 ||
The essential meaning:
Some, devoid of discernment yet renowned for their prowess, roam the world like manifest piśācas.
What should I employ here according to my usual nature?
It is well known that envy is the preeminent quality of the noble. (16) The essential meaning (*bhāvārtha*): [The Hindi commentary was not digitized.]
Having reflected thus within myself as a teacher, and having relaxed my envy,
I shall set forth the scripture according to its proper application.

Issued from the mouth of the Omniscient One, received by Gaṇadeva, and subsequently descended through the lineage of great sages. (17) The meaning of the intent: [The Hindi commentary was not digitized.]

"Stinginess is known to be shunned by the assembly of noble ones"—this is an alternative reading. A stingy person is avoided by virtuous men; this is well-known in the world. [Now follows] the etymological derivation of the word "physician" (*vaidya*).

"Vidyā" is the name for the true, manifest, and absolute eye; those who know the specific distinctions of words and scriptures declare that this noble scripture, which is established therein, is "vaidya."

Reflecting upon this, those physicians also recite it. (18) The essential meaning (*bhāvārtha*): [The meaning of the term *Āyurveda*] (Note: The provided Hindi commentary was not digitized. The meaning of the word *Āyurveda*: [To be supplied].
And because of attaining the investigation of consciousness through the thought "this is the Veda," his speech indeed indicates the true meaning due to the distinction of the elements;
and by that, his previously bound lifespan arises.
Those who know the truth proclaim another title for this scripture. 19. The essential meaning:—The promise to describe the qualities and characteristics of a disciple.
Those who have been fashioned here as vessels for such a physician— who is uniquely preeminent in promoting the welfare of the world—
are characterized by a resemblance to the qualities of the virtuous.
We shall now speak [of those] who have set out upon the path followed by the Lord of Jinas. (20) The meaning of the intent (*bhāvārtha*):
[A disciple fit for the study of Āyurveda]. (Note: The Hindi commentary was not digitized.)
A certain wise man of irreproachable conduct, skilled and humble, born into a family of kshatriyas, brahmins, or vaishyas,
should approach his teacher in the morning and inquire as follows.
Thus, he shall become a partaker of the stainless discipline of the scriptures.
(21) The essential meaning: [The sequence for the gift of the science of medicine]. (Note: The Hindi commentary was not digitized.)
This preeminent scripture should always be given to one who is known for his virtues, who has been thoroughly examined, and who has undertaken the true vows in the presence of an Arhat.
"Those who know the science of medicine say that it must not be given to anyone else. The essential meaning (*bhāvārtha*)—[The Hindi commentary was not digitized.
The means for acquiring knowledge (*vidyāprāpti-sādhana*).

The teacher, the means of accomplishment, the companions, the dwelling, and the consort; health, intelligence, discipline, diligence, and devotion to the scriptures— these are the means for accomplishing one's own internal and external virtuous qualities.
These have been thus constantly illustrated for those seeking the meaning of the scriptures. (23) The essential meaning is: the primary objective of the science of medicine.
Indeed, this treatise is for the purpose of benefiting the world;
furthermore, the purpose of the treatise is twofold:
namely, the protection of the healthy and the liberation from disease.

In brief, everything is described here. (24) [The meaning of the word *loka*: **Bhāvārtha:** The Hindi commentary has not been digitized. [The meaning of the word *loka*: The term *loka* refers to the world or the realm of beings. It denotes the sphere of existence where living entities dwell, encompassing both the physical universe and the various states of consciousness experienced therein. In this context, it signifies the entire field of manifestation, including the realms of gods, humans, animals, and those in lower states of being. Thus, "the whole" (*sakalam*) refers to the totality of these diverse worlds and their inhabitants.

For in that [scripture], they instantly perceive the six categories of existent things, beginning with the living beings (jīva), which are distinguished by the divisions of stationary and moving entities, and which possess their own inherent qualities, classes, and essential natures.
This world is thus regarded by the ancient sages. (25) [The essential meaning: The foundations of medical treatment.

According to the established doctrine, among the five types of excellent sense-faculties known as "perfected" (*paryāpta*), which are distinguished by the various classifications of living beings (*jīva-samāsa*),
human beings who are devoted to the Dharma are the foremost.
And in a field abounding in righteousness, those born for the ultimate truth [attain it]. 26.
The meaning of the state [is as follows]:—The Hindi commentary was not digitized.
Their treatment is performed daily by physicians.

Having understood, in their proper sequence, the lifespan, age, digestive fire, strength, mental faculty, location, suitability, the well-known types of constitution, the drugs, the body, the diseases, and the stages of time; || 27 ||
The essential meaning:
The four pillars of medical treatment are described therein by the sages as "kriyā" (action).

This [treatment] consists of four types of entities, in which the physician, the patient, the medicine, and the group of good attendants are the constituent factors; among these, the physician alone is primary, possessing complete wisdom. (28)
The essential meaning:
A physician should possess the characteristics of a scholar, be endowed with wisdom regarding the meaning of the texts, and be proficient in other systems of thought.
Skilled in correct application, adept, exceedingly steadfast,
preeminent in dharma, well-conducted, and purified by many sacred rites, such a physician would be worthy of the wise and the great. || 29 ||
The essential meaning:
[This is determined] through inquiries regarding the method of medical treatment, by means of the rules of omens, and by the arrival of auspicious signs.

Having ascertained the measure of the lifespan of the afflicted through specific planetary configurations, the positions of the moon at the ascendant, and even divine dreams described in the scriptures, the physician should apply himself to his task.
The essential meaning is this:
in this world, the death of a living being does not occur without some calamity (riṣṭa),
whether it be through the displacement from its natural state or by something extremely subtle.

A physician should examine even those difficult cases here, which manifest in the forms of the past, present, and future, by means of diligent methods. (31) The essential meaning (*bhāvārtha*): [The Hindi commentary was not digitized.]
The signs of *ariṣṭa* (fatal omens) consist in the reversal of the natural characteristics of one's constitution, body, innate nature, complexion, form, and excellent features.
Furthermore, a transformation of the objects of the five senses, and the sinking of feces or phlegm into water, are causes for the death of the patient.
The essential meaning (*bhāvārtha*)— the Hindi commentary has not been digitized.
One who possesses the characteristics of an ill-omened messenger—having limbs that are deficient, redundant, excessively emaciated, black, or parched;
being afflicted by disease himself; or having a weapon or a staff in hand.
At the twilights, with tearful eyes and trembling with fear,
the messenger becomes exceedingly like a messenger of Yama;
[he arrives] with horses, donkeys, excellent chariots, young camels, and superior vehicles.
The host of messengers always becomes exceedingly censurable for one who,
standing at the front, cuts grass, splits wood, or breaks clods of earth, straw, or bricks.
Having thus suddenly observed such an omen manifested by a messenger— a sign that is the sole cause for the death of the patient—
the physician who understands the meaning of the medical scriptures should avoid treating him here.

An auspicious messenger, characterized by gentle features, dressed in clean garments, and belonging to one's own caste, brings about welfare. (35) The meaning of the intent (bhāvārtha): [The Hindi commentary was not digitized.]
Inauspicious omens,
agitation, the obstruction of the rising sign (*lagna*), the affliction of enemies, stumbling through rivalry, and great suffering through anger.
Village raids, quarrels, the outbreak of fire, and similar events must certainly be avoided by physicians at the time of departure. 36.
[The meaning of the intent: The Hindi commentary was not digitized.
A cat, a snake, a rabbit, a porcupine, a log,
a stream of water, fire, a boar, a buffalo, mongooses, jackals, red garlands, and the dirty loads of a washerman.
Those who have arrived from Samataka should be avoided. (37) The essential meaning—[The Hindi commentary was not digitized.
Auspicious Omen.
When the quarters are peaceful, there are auspicious omens: the sounds of drums, large kettledrums, conchs, clouds, excellent flutes, and clay drums;
as well as parasols, banners, a prince, white garments, and maidens.
There were gentle, fragrant breezes favorable to song;
white unbroken rice, lotuses, peacocks, and blue-throated birds;
women graceful with playful charms; and lordly elephants.
Jars filled with clear water and bulls or horses facing forward at the time of departure are auspicious. (39) The essential meaning (*bhāvārtha*)— [The Hindi commentary was not digitized].
Thus, having observed a patient whose limbs are marked with excellent characteristics and who possesses the glory described in the section on great omens,
the physician should here deliberate upon his supreme lifespan.
One should observe how much has already passed and how much remains yet to come.
(40) The essential meaning—[The examination of short and long lifespans according to the Sāmudrika Śāstra]. The Hindi commentary was not digitized.
Whose two [feet] are exceedingly tender, very fleshy, smooth, resembling the sprouts of an *aśoka* tree and a lotus,
and endowed with various beautiful, firm, broad, and long [features].
His hands and feet here are marked with lines and stainless;
his ears are exceedingly delicate and large,
his eyes have the luster of blue lotuses, and his teeth are likewise [beautiful].
He whose forehead, hair, and face are smooth, elevated, and broad, resembling a pomegranate seed that is always liberated [from its rind];
he whose breath, eyes, and arms are long and well-developed.
The fingers, nails, face, and nose should be thick;
the tongue, sense organs, throat, belly, penis, and shanks should be short; and the joints, the opening of the anus, the navel, and the ankles should be deep-set. || 43 ||
One whose chest is very broad, or for whom the distance between the breasts or the eyebrows is wide, and whose network of veins is restrained and hidden;
one whose body, when anointed or smeared with unguents here, remains only upright.
Then his body, and finally even his head, would wither away;
for his body, which has been free from disease since birth, gradually and constantly undergoes growth.
He whose intellect is sufficiently powerful to comprehend even the entire collection of training rules (śikṣākalāpa), whose faculties are all firm,
and who possesses a mass of hair that is very glossy, fine, and soft— [he is one who has attained the fruit]. 45.
One whose body is generally such that the hair-pores are sparse and marked with irreproachable, auspicious signs, possesses abundant wealth and an exceedingly long life. (46)
Thus, by means of all these auspicious marks,
a man shall be long-lived; otherwise, his life will be short, as it is known that for one who possesses contrary characteristics, the lifespan is reduced by half.
Therefore, this sound health is considered to be the prime of life. 47.
[The meaning of the verse: The Hindi commentary was not digitized. Conclusion.
Thus, one whose intellect has crossed to the further shore of the vast ocean of sacred learning,
having understood that [disease] and first investigating the lifespan of the patient here, being possessed of exalted glory,
should again exert effort both in discerning the true nature of the disease and in its suppression.

A physician who knows the rules should perform [this] daily, preserving his own stainless reputation. (48) The Essential Meaning (*bhāvārtha*): [This concludes the section from] the great ocean of the excellent scriptures that have emerged from the power of the Jinas.
Agitated by the multitude of waves spread across all categories of objects,
and radiant with its two shores that accomplish the goals of both worlds, this [teaching] has indeed issued forth like a spray of water for the singular benefit of the universe. (49)
The meaning of the essence—[the Hindi commentary was not digitized].
Now begins the second chapter: the auspicious invocation and the formal declaration of intent.

Having bowed to the Jina, the cause of the destruction of all karma without exception, who is worshipped by the hosts of gods and asuras, I shall therefore speak of that which is characterized by the investigation of well-being, as it is defined by the wise through its true characteristics. The meaning of the intent (bhāvārtha): [The Hindi commentary was not digitized.]
Now, regarding the types of well-being for a fortunate man here and now, that well-being has been declared by the Jinas to be of two kinds:
the first is the primary, which is the ultimate reality (*paramārtha*); the second is the other, which arises from conventional usage (*vyavahāra*). (2)
The essential meaning:
This supreme, wonderful state, characterized by ultimate well-being and born from the total destruction of all karma, is absolute and without a second.
That which is beyond the senses is sought by those who know the true goal; this very thing is called the "Ultimate Reality" (paramārtha). [The meaning of the verse:
The characteristic of the well-being of worldly conduct (*vyavahāra*). *Bhāvārtha:* [The Hindi commentary was not digitized.]

The state of equilibrium of the bodily constituents (*dhātu*), freedom from the confusion of the humors (*doṣa*), the proper functioning of the organs of excretion, the clarity of the sense faculties, and constant serenity of mind in a person— this indeed is what has been described as arising from worldly conduct (*vyavahāra*). The essential meaning (*bhāvārtha*)— the Hindi commentary was not digitized.

"One whose humors are in equilibrium, whose digestive fire is balanced, whose bodily constituents, excretions, and functions are normal, and whose self, senses, and mind are serene, is designated as healthy," says Vāgbhaṭa.
The state of being very gentle through the investigation of equilibrium is indeed called *sāmya* (equilibrium). Appetite, digestion, and strength are its characteristics;
the practice of moderate diet is its means; and the attainment of the four goals of life is considered its strength. (5)

The essential meaning: What is the use of verbal deliberation regarding those who know the true purpose of life and who possess specific excellence in physical strength and form? Those who truly understand them observe their equality and declare it as such, rather than saying "this one is like this" or "that one is like that" in various ways. 6.
The essential meaning:

What is the definition of being established in one's own nature (*svastha*)? It is characterized by the reflection of one who is established in their own nature; it occurs when a person becomes free from diseases.

At that very moment, he is proclaimed to be established in his own nature (*svastha*); there is nothing whatsoever other than the path of the scriptures. 7. The essential meaning (*bhāvārtha*)—[the Hindi commentary was not digitized].
Consideration of the states (*avasthā-vicāra*).

The Victors have classified age into four types: childhood, youth, middle age, and old age. Thus, through ten decades [of years] combined, a person in the Kali Yuga has a lifespan of one hundred years. The essential meaning (bhāvārtha): [The Hindi commentary was not digitized.]
The functions of the stages [of life] are tenfold: childhood, growth, exuberance, youth,
and likewise that which is accompanied by the excellence of skin, bone, shell-like purity, and prowess, through the withdrawal of the primary intellect and the senses.
—*Tvagakṣi* is an alternative reading; the meaning of the term *bhāva* is as follows: Consideration regarding food during a change of state.

Now, some child eats only milk; another eats milk with rice; and yet another eats fine food—thus is the threefold rule of diet for young people. Among others, however, a sumptuous feast alone is considered excellent. The essential meaning (bhāvārtha): [The Hindi commentary was not digitized.]

The physician should carefully examine the digestive fire (jaṭharāgni) in those of middle age or even the elderly, and perform the treatment progressively, having properly assessed the strength of the individual's internal fire and its state of equilibrium or imbalance according to the scriptures. || 11 ||
The meaning of the essence—

here too, the fire of the digestive organ (*jaṭharāgni*) is explained as being threefold according to its modifications. Due to the humors (*doṣas*), it becomes irregular (*viṣama*) or excessively sharp (*atitīkṣṇa*).

The qualities [of the humors] are also [described], along with the mild wind (vāta), bile (pitta), and phlegm (kapha); their respective treatments will now be explained here in due order. Bhāvārtha: The treatment for impaired digestion (vibamāgni) and other conditions.

Then, by means of enemas, effective purgatives, as well as suitable emetics and nasal medications, the physician should gradually cure abdominal enlargements and impaired digestive fires caused by the affliction of Vāta, Pitta, and Kapha. The essential meaning (bhāvārtha): [The Hindi commentary was not digitized.]
The means for protecting balanced *agni*:

An intelligent person should always protect the balanced *agni* through the application of dietary rules, as well as by means of enemas suitable for the three periods of the day, purgatives, and emetics. (14)
The essential meaning:
A man, though emaciated, may be strong; even one who is very weak may exist as someone quite stout.

In this world, the strength of men must be examined in many ways—even by means of running and other such activities, despite great burdens. (15) The essential meaning: [The Hindi commentary was not digitized.
The Primacy of Strength.
Strength is indeed the foremost factor in all medical procedures; therefore, a wise physician should carefully examine the strength of the patients.

One who desires a successful outcome with ease should perform the treatment only upon those who possess superior strength in this world. (16) The essential meaning (*bhāvārtha*): [The Hindi commentary was not digitized.]

The internal cause for the arising of strength is always the supreme goodness of character (*susattva*) in a striving person, which results from the subsiding, the destruction, or the subsiding-and-destruction of one's own karmas. One who possesses such goodness of character endures the various hardships (*parīṣaha*). (17)
That which properly digests food consumed in the appropriate quantity is called *samāgni*. **The Meaning:** The characteristics of a strong person.
He is truly possessed of courage who, even in the face of prosperity or decline, maintains a posture with a blossoming and serene lotus-like countenance;
his mind, resting upon fortitude, is not pierced by even the most unbearable of specific actions. (18) The Essential Meaning (Bhāvārtha): [The Hindi commentary was not digitized.]

The three types of regions, beginning with Jāṅgala, are known by their respective names: Jāṅgala, Anūpa, and Sādhāraṇa. Furthermore, another [classification] is always proclaimed as threefold: Pradhāna, Sādhāraṇa, and [the third]. I shall now state the characteristics of these three in due order. (19)
The essential meaning—[The characteristics of the Jāṅgala country:
In some places there are dry grasses, crops, and creepers; and in other places there are trees such as the Sarja, Arjuna, and Bhūrja.
In some places there were palāśa trees with branches laden with leaves; in others, the ground was red, black, or pale.
In some places there were mountains covered with rough stones; in others, forests thick with bamboo and hollows.
In some places there were fierce tigers, wolves, bears, and wild beasts; and in others, parched iron pyrites mixed with gravel.
In some places there were excellent priyaṅgu plants and kodrava grains; in others, o Śāntanu, there were mudga beans and chickpeas.
In some places there were herds of donkeys, horses, cattle, and camels; in others, flocks of sheep along with large groups of goats.
And in some places, far outside the wretched villages, there were great, bottomless, and most terrifying pits.
In those regions, water in wells is always extremely difficult to obtain; people extract it with great effort using mechanical contrivances.

There, the people are naturally very emaciated, covered with prominent veins, rigid, harsh, and possessing gaunt frames; they are also constantly afflicted by diseases caused by wind (vāta). Therefore, one should practice measures that pacify the wind for them.
The essential meaning— The characteristics of the *anūpa* region have thus been described, as well as those of the *jāṅgala*; thereafter, the classification of the *anūpa* is further explained.
In due order, for there the earth is always cool with water and difficult to traverse because of its mud;

where, by its very nature, the grasses, shrubs, bushes, and spreading creepers are exceedingly tender; and where there are banyan trees, *viṭaṅka* trees, and magnificent *pāṭalī* trees, as well as *pārijātaka* trees strewn with heaps of blossoms. || 25–26 ||
Where there are always Aśoka, Kakkola, Laṃvaka, Kaṅguka, Vilāsa, Jātī, Varajāti, and Mallikā trees, as well as Mādhavī creepers; where the Mālatī vines are thick with trembling flowers;
and where the mountains, their peaks washed by the gods, are adorned with great trees.
Where the *caṃpaka* trees tremble under the heavy rain of thunderclouds, and the mango and *ketaka* trees are filled with the cries of peacocks;

where there are *tamāla*, *tālī*, and excellent *nālikera* trees, and in succession rows of *kramuka* trees, always surrounded by forests of *tāla* and *hiṃtāla*; where lakes and rivers are exceedingly beautiful with their clear waters. (28–29)
Where the lakes, ponds, and rivers always resemble fragments of the autumnal sky,
adorned with clusters of lotuses and water-lilies tossed by cranes, swans, and wild cocks;
where there are everywhere spreading creepers of hanging betel vines, and fields of ripening rice on all sides.
The groves of plantain trees, radiant with their surrounding thickets of great sugarcane, are beautiful;

there is an abundance of bright buffalo curds resembling ripe cow's milk, along with jackfruit, mangoes, and jujube, scattered with dates and coconuts, and delicious food with plenty of molasses. (31-32)
In that place, people are always characterized by an abundance of *mārdava* (gentleness), possess delicate and radiant hands and feet,
have extremely stout bodily constitutions, are dominated by *kapha*, and are afflicted with diseases caused by *vāta*. Consequently,
physicians there invariably administer treatments for both *kapha* and *vāta*.

Thus has the procedure for the Ānūpa region been proclaimed; likewise, the discourse regarding the characteristics of the Sādhāraṇa region [is as follows]. (34) —An alternative reading is "mahēkṣuvāṭī"; the meaning of the subject matter is as follows.
The characteristics of a suitable location are as follows:
the ground is not excessively red, nor is it pale; it is neither too dry nor too dense;
there is neither excessive cold nor harsh heat; there is neither excessive wind nor extraordinary rain. (35)

In this world, there is no counting of mountains, nor is it a forest of gods; here the earth is not entirely devoid of hills, nor is it excessively watery, nor is it parched with lack of water; there are no excessive thieves, nor are there wicked or evil beasts.
This world possesses excellent crops and abounds in virtuous people, owing to the proper application of seasonal food and sustenance.
Due to the equilibrium of the digestive fire (*agni*), there is no provocation of the humors (*doṣa*) and consequently no disease at all times.

Therefore, that which possesses the characteristics of both regions is indeed excellent; because people dwell there in constant happiness, the sequence of wholesome suitability (*susātmyakrama*) is now described. (37–38)
The essential meaning:
Consideration of suitability for a person;
suitable medicinal substances; and the primary factors of country, water, disease, and physical constitution.
Whatever else is conducive to happiness, when practiced [in excess], it becomes contrary; otherwise, it remains so. (39) The essential meaning: Every substance can become wholesome (*sātmya*).

When poison is consumed in very small quantities gradually and is digested regularly, it does not cause any harm to a person; rather, within seven days, it becomes habituated to the body (sātmyaka). **The Essential Meaning:** [The Hindi commentary has not been digitized.]
Having declared the promise to describe the *prakṛti* (nature),

[the author], after explaining the characteristics of effort and suitability, will thoroughly explain the *prakṛti* of men along with the characteristics of the embryo, based on recognized causes such as the recollection of previous births. (41)
The essential meaning:
A woman who has reached her fertile period, observing the vow of a sage during her season, having discarded her garlands, ornaments, and unguents— [should approach her husband].

During the day, she should eat from a leaf-plate or with her cupped hands; at night, she should likewise sleep upon a bed of *darbha* grass. (42) The meaning of the intent (*bhāvārtha*)—[Note: The Hindi commentary was not digitized.
The Procedure for Conception (*garbhādhāna-krama*).

The husband should avoid her for three days. Then, on the fourth day, she has been auspiciously bathed with immersions in water, adorned with auspicious rites, and is radiant; he should provide her with a meal of *kṛśara* rice mixed with oil while it is still warm. He himself should consume a meal consisting of abundant, highly aphrodisiac foods blended with ghee, milk, and molasses.
Well-adorned, with a virtuous mind,
he should go at night to that beautiful woman, the captivating wife of Manohara, if there is a desire for a son from them.
Pressing his right side against the woman’s body, he should lie down for a moment on her other side.
The meaning of the verse:
At the time of menstruation,
a woman who has conceived may, due to ignorance, [act in such a way that] she might become one who has conceived on the very first day.
This offspring dies from its own womb on the second night, or even within the period of birth-impurity (sūtaka);
or it may die again on the third night; or it may become stammering, blind, deaf, or extremely mute by nature, or even exceedingly cruel; therefore, one should introduce the seed on the fourth day.
